title: Actor Model & Message Passing
tagline: Concurrent systems without shared mutable state

sections.content:
The **Actor Model**, introduced by Carl Hewitt in 1973, is a mathematical model for concurrent computation. Its central insight: eliminate shared mutable state entirely. Instead of threads competing for locks on shared data, each **actor** is an independent unit that owns its state exclusively and communicates solely by **sending messages** to other actors' mailboxes.

This model powers Erlang (WhatsApp's legendary 2 million connections per server), Akka (JVM actors), and Elixir. It makes reasoning about concurrent systems dramatically simpler because race conditions and deadlocks — the two plagues of shared-memory concurrency — cannot arise when no memory is shared.

sections.title: The Office Department Analogy
sections.content:
Imagine a company where each **department** (actor) has its own locked filing cabinet (private state) and an **in-tray** on the desk (mailbox). Departments never walk into each other's offices to rearrange files — that would cause chaos. Instead, they send **memos** (messages) to another department's in-tray.

The receiving department processes memos one at a time when it has capacity. It can:
1. **Update its own files** (mutate local state).
2. **Send memos to other departments** (send messages).
3. **Create new departments** (spawn child actors).

Because each department only touches its own cabinet, there are no file conflicts — no locks needed. If a department catches fire (crashes), a supervisor department gets notified and can restart it. This is Erlang's **"let it crash"** philosophy: build supervision trees instead of defensive error handling.

sections.title: Actor Primitives and Supervision Trees
sections.content:
Every actor can do exactly three things in response to a message:
- **Send** messages to actors it has addresses (PIDs) for.
- **Create** new child actors.
- **Update** its own private state for processing the next message.

Actors process messages **sequentially** from their mailbox — one at a time, no concurrency within a single actor. This eliminates all intra-actor race conditions. Concurrency arises from having many actors processing their own mailboxes simultaneously across CPU cores.

**Location transparency** is a key feature: an actor's address (PID) works the same whether the target actor is on the same process, same machine, or a remote server. This makes distribution trivial — you scale horizontally by running actors on more nodes without changing communication code.

**Message passing vs shared memory:**
- **Shared memory** requires locks, condition variables, and careful coordination. Correctness depends on every thread following the protocol perfectly — one mistake causes a race.
- **Message passing** requires no locks. State is implicit in each actor's current behavior. The tradeoff is message serialization cost and higher latency for what would be a simple pointer dereference in shared memory.

The **supervision tree** in Erlang/OTP and Akka structures actors hierarchically. A supervisor monitors its children and applies a restart strategy (one-for-one, one-for-all, rest-for-one) when a child crashes. This isolates failure and enables self-healing systems — core to WhatsApp and Ericsson telecom switch uptime of 99.9999999%.

sections.caption: Supervision tree: when Worker C crashes, only the supervisor is notified. It restarts the failed child without affecting siblings.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: Each `Worker` is an actor: it owns `state` privately (no other actor can read or write it), and communicates exclusively via `postMessage` (message passing). `actor1` and `actor2` operate independently — no locks, no shared variables. The main thread acts as a lightweight supervisor.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: **When to choose message passing over shared memory:** prefer message passing when tasks are naturally independent (request handlers, pipeline stages, microservices) or when you need fault isolation and restartability. Use shared memory (`SharedArrayBuffer` + `Atomics`) only for tight inner loops where message serialization latency is unacceptable — e.g., real-time audio processing or scientific simulation inner loops.

items: An **actor** is an independent unit of computation with private state, a mailbox, and the ability to send messages, spawn children, and update its own state.
**No shared state** means no locks, no deadlocks, and no race conditions between actors — all safety comes from the exclusive ownership model.
Actors process their mailbox **sequentially**, so each actor is race-free internally; concurrency arises from many actors running simultaneously.
**Supervision trees** (Erlang/OTP, Akka) structure actors hierarchically — supervisors restart crashed children, enabling self-healing distributed systems.
**Location transparency** allows actor addresses to work identically whether the target is local or remote, making horizontal scaling a first-class concern.

quiz.question: What are the three things an actor can do in response to a received message?
options: Lock a mutex, read shared memory, and write shared memory
Send messages to known actors, create new actors, and update its own private state
Spawn a thread, block on I/O, and release a lock
Read shared state, modify it, and notify other threads
quiz.explanation: The Actor Model defines exactly three response capabilities: send messages to actors whose addresses (PIDs) are known, create new child actors, and update private local state to influence how future messages are handled.

quiz.question: Why does the Actor Model eliminate race conditions between actors?
options: Actors use internal mutexes automatically
Actors share read-only memory and lock before writing
Each actor owns its state exclusively and no actor can access another's state directly
The runtime enforces a global lock on all state changes
quiz.explanation: Because actors never share memory, there is nothing to race on. An actor's state can only be modified by that actor itself as it processes messages sequentially. Other actors can only request changes by sending messages.

quiz.question: What is 'location transparency' in the Actor Model?
options: All actors must run on the same physical machine
An actor's address works the same whether the target is local or on a remote server
Messages are cached locally before being sent remotely
Actors are transparent to the OS scheduler
quiz.explanation: Location transparency means actor addresses (PIDs, references) are uniform regardless of physical location. Code sending a message to a local actor is identical to code sending to a remote actor — enabling distribution without changing application logic.

quiz.question: In Erlang's 'let it crash' philosophy, what should an actor do when it encounters an unexpected error?
options: Catch all exceptions and log them internally
Retry the failed operation up to 3 times
Crash immediately, letting the supervisor handle restart with a clean state
Notify all sibling actors before terminating
quiz.explanation: 'Let it crash' means actors should not attempt complex defensive error recovery. An unexpected crash is reported up the supervision tree. The supervisor restarts the actor with a fresh state, which is often simpler and more reliable than trying to recover from unknown bad state.

quiz.question: How do actors achieve concurrency if each actor processes messages sequentially?
options: They cannot — sequential processing means no concurrency
They use async/await internally to interleave message handling
Thousands of actors each process their own mailboxes simultaneously across cores
A global thread pool processes all actor mailboxes in round-robin order
quiz.explanation: Concurrency in the Actor Model comes from having many actors, each running independently. While each actor is sequential internally (processing one message at a time), many actors run concurrently across CPU cores, achieving massive parallelism without any shared state.

quiz.question: What restart strategy does 'one-for-one' supervision apply when a child actor crashes?
options: Restart all child actors regardless of which one crashed
Restart only the crashed child actor
Terminate all children and the supervisor itself
Restart all children that were started after the crashed one
quiz.explanation: 'One-for-one' restarts only the specific child that crashed, leaving all siblings running. This is the least disruptive strategy and appropriate when actors are independent. 'One-for-all' restarts all siblings when any one crashes.

quiz.question: What is the primary advantage of message passing over shared memory concurrency?
options: Lower memory usage
No need for locks, eliminating deadlocks and race conditions
Faster execution due to less copying
Simpler CPU cache behavior
quiz.explanation: Message passing eliminates shared mutable state, so there is nothing to lock. With no locks, there can be no deadlocks (circular lock waiting) or data races (concurrent unsynchronized access). The tradeoff is serialization overhead for messages.

quiz.question: Which real-world system famously demonstrated the Actor Model's scalability at 2 million concurrent connections on a single server?
options: Redis using an event loop
WhatsApp using Erlang
Nginx using OS threads
Kafka using the Reactor pattern
quiz.explanation: WhatsApp used Erlang's actor-based concurrency to achieve 2 million simultaneous connections on a single server at their peak. Erlang's lightweight actor processes (not OS threads) and supervision trees made this scale feasible.

quiz.question: When is shared memory (`SharedArrayBuffer` + Atomics) preferred over message passing in JavaScript?
options: For all inter-worker communication
When building supervision trees
For tight inner loops where serialization latency is unacceptable
When location transparency is required
quiz.explanation: Message passing serializes data (structured clone algorithm) which adds latency and CPU cost. For performance-critical inner loops — real-time audio, scientific computation — sharing a `SharedArrayBuffer` between workers avoids serialization, at the cost of requiring explicit Atomic operations.

quiz.question: An actor receives a 'GET' request and responds with a copy of its internal counter value. Why is returning a copy important?
options: Copies are faster to transmit than references
Returning a reference would expose the actor's private state, allowing external mutation
The Actor Model requires all messages to be serialized to JSON
Copies prevent garbage collection issues
quiz.explanation: Returning a reference (pointer) to internal state would allow the recipient to modify that state directly, bypassing the actor's message-based access control. Returning a copy (or immutable value) preserves the invariant that only the actor itself can mutate its own state.
